method: Rebuild from primary text. Cal. Civ. Code §1542, Cal. Lab. Code §206.5 (read within the Division 2 Part 1 Chapter 1 Article 1 text view), Cal. Lab. Code §5001, Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code §1342 and Cal. Gov. Code §12964.5 were all fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and read; Winet v. Price was read on CourtListener. The clause asserted four separate limits on what an employee release can waive and cited only §1542, which contains none of them; each limit was traced to its own section. Assertions describe the REBUILT body.
queries: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code §1342 full text (leginfo)

assertions.text: the substance of §1542 as amended effective 1 January 2019
what decides the waiver is conscious understanding, not the form of words
assertions.note: Winet v. Price, restating Casey v. Proctor. The previous body's 'quoting it, or unknown claims survive' states a drafting convention as a rule.

assertions.text: a release of wages due is null and void unless those wages have been paid, and requiring one is a misdemeanour
assertions.note: Lab. Code §206.5(a), verbatim: 'An employer shall not require the execution of a release of a claim or right on account of wages due, or to become due, or made as an advance on wages to be earned, unless payment of those wages has been made. A release required or executed in violation of the provisions of this section shall be null and void as between the employer and the employee. Violation of this section by the employer is a misdemeanor.' The previous body asserted this and cited §1542.

assertions.text: no release or compromise of a workers' compensation claim is valid unless approved by the appeals board or a referee
assertions.note: Lab. Code §5001, verbatim. Not merely that the claim 'cannot be waived' — the mechanism is approval, which a drafter needs to know.

assertions.text: any waiver of a benefit or right under the Unemployment Insurance Code is invalid, and benefits are not subject to assignment, release or commutation
assertions.note: Unemp. Ins. Code §1342, with the enumerated exceptions in §§1255.7, 1342.1, 1345 and 2630.

assertions.text: a separation agreement may not prohibit disclosure of information about unlawful acts in the workplace, and a non-disparagement or workplace-conditions restriction must carry the prescribed language in substantial form
assertions.note: Gov. Code §12964.5(b)(1)(A)-(B) as amended by Stats. 2021, Ch. 638 (SB 331), including the required sentence quoted verbatim in the clause body. §12964.5(c) defines 'information about unlawful acts in the workplace' to include conduct the employee has reasonable cause to believe is unlawful, which is where the previous body's phrasing came from.

assertions.text: a general release of all claims is still permitted in a separation agreement, the severance amount may still be kept confidential, and trade secrets not involving unlawful acts may still be protected
assertions.note: §12964.5(b)(3), (e) and (f). All three were absent from the previous body, which stated only prohibitions and so read as though a separation release were largely unavailable.

assertions.text: the employer must notify the employee of the right to consult an attorney and give at least five business days, which the employee may shorten only knowingly and voluntarily and without inducement
assertions.note: §12964.5(b)(4), verbatim in substance including the four kinds of inducement it names. This is a requirement the clause never had at all, and it is procedural — an employer that gets everything else right and skips it has an unlawful practice.

priorDefects: uncited: four asserted limits (wages, workers' compensation, unemployment benefits, agency participation) were all attributed to Civ. Code §1542, which contains none of them.

overstated: 'cannot ... waive the right to file with or participate in an agency investigation'. Gov. Code §12964.5(a)(1)(A)(ii) forbids requiring that release in exchange for a raise or bonus or as a condition of employment or continued employment; §12964.5(b)(3) permits a general release in a separation agreement and §12964.5(d)(1) takes negotiated settlements of filed claims outside the section.
contradicted: 'quoting it, or unknown claims survive' — the consequence is not automatic and the quotation is not the operative act.
omitted: §12964.5(b)(4), the notice of the right to consult counsel and the five business days.
omitted: the prescribed 'Nothing in this agreement prevents you...' language.
omitted: that a general release is still permitted, that the severance amount may be kept confidential, and that trade secret protection survives.
omitted: that the workers' compensation limit works by requiring appeals board approval rather than by outright prohibition.
gaps: The Older Workers Benefit Protection Act was not read. Its consideration and revocation periods for an age-discrimination waiver are longer than the five business days §12964.5(b)(4) requires, so an employer following this clause for an employee over forty would be short. This is the most serious thing left in the clause.
Code of Civil Procedure §1001, which restricts confidentiality provisions in settlements of certain harassment and discrimination claims, was not read and overlaps §12964.5.

Gov. Code §12964.5(a), which governs what an employer may require at hire or in exchange for a raise, was read but is not carried into the body — the clause is about separation. An employer that reads only this clause will not learn the rule that applies at the front of the relationship.
Whether a release may waive claims under the Private Attorneys General Act was not researched.
Casey v. Proctor was read only as quoted in Winet.

judicialQuotations.quote: its purpose was to prevent the mere recital in the release to that effect from barring a claim for injuries later discovered in the absence of a showing of a conscious understanding...

note: Gov. Code §12964.5 is the section that makes this clause work, and it did not appear in the clause's sources before this rebuild. It both narrows what a separation release may say and adds a procedural step. No decision construing it was searched for; it dates from 2018 and was amended in 2021, so there may be little.
